## Explicit Euler method

In Section 3, we showed which equilibria are stable or unstable when $I=0$. Now, we want to see how the coordination preference $x$ changes over time. Indeed, while the stability analysis in Section 3 tells us where the preference ends up, the simulation shows how and how fast it gets there. To do so, we will use the explicit Euler method.

The explicit Euler method is a numerical technique that calculates how $x$ changes by taking small steps forward in time. The formula for the Euler method is:

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n + h \, f(x_n)
$$

where $x_n$ is the current preference, $x_{n+1}$ is the preference at the next step, $h$ is the size of the time step, and $f(x_n)$ is the rate of change (speed) at the current step. It is an explicit method because the right-hand side of the equation is already known. Indeed, we calculate the next preference ($x_{n+1}$) based on the current preference ($x_n$), so this method is direct. When applying this method to our model, we get:

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n + h \left( 1.2\,x_n - 0.8\,x_n^{3} + I \right)
$$

The simulation settings are taken from the assignment [@course2026] and are summarized in @tbl-settings. The only difference between the two simulations is the starting value.

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Instruction | $I = 0$ |
| Time step | $h = 0.01$ |
| Simulation time | $t \in [0, 20]$ |
| Initial preferences | $x(0) = -1.8$ and $x(0) = +1.8$ |

: Simulation settings [@course2026]. {#tbl-settings}

These starting values are not chosen randomly. One lies on the Pattern A side and the other on the Pattern B side of the unstable equilibrium at $x = 0$. This allows us to check whether the two simulations reach different stable equilibria, as predicted by the stability analysis in Section 3.

## Long-term behaviour

```{python}
I = 0.0                                        # no external instruction
h = 0.01                                       # time step (called dt in Lab 2)
t0, t_end = 0.0, 20.0                          # start and end of the simulation
n_steps = int(round((t_end - t0) / h))         # number of Euler steps: 20 / 0.01 = 2000 (same as Lab 2)

t = np.linspace(t0, t_end, n_steps + 1)        # 2001 time values: 0, 0.01, 0.02, ..., 20 (the +1 is the starting point)

x_A = np.zeros(n_steps + 1)                    # preference over time, starting on the Pattern A side
x_B = np.zeros(n_steps + 1)                    # preference over time, starting on the Pattern B side
x_A[0] = -1.8                                  # initial condition x(0) = -1.8
x_B[0] = 1.8                                   # initial condition x(0) = +1.8
```

```{python}
for n in range(n_steps):                       # repeat for each of the 2000 time steps
    x_A[n + 1] = x_A[n] + h * f(x_A[n], I)     # new value = old value + step size * rate of change at the old value
    x_B[n + 1] = x_B[n] + h * f(x_B[n], I)     # same Euler update for the second starting value
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-baseline-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "Euler simulations of the preference $x(t)$ for $I = 0$ and $h = 0.01$, starting from $x(0) = -1.8$ and $x(0) = +1.8$ (dots). Dashed lines show the stable equilibria $x \\approx \\pm 1.225$ found in Section 3; the grey line shows the unstable equilibrium $x = 0$."

eq = equilibrium_points(I)                     # the 3 equilibria for I = 0: -1.225, 0, +1.225
stable = (f(eq - 0.01, I) > 0) & (f(eq + 0.01, I) < 0)  # True for stable equilibria (same test as Section 3)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))         # creates the figure (6 x 4 inches) and the axes
ax.plot(t, x_A, color="tab:blue", label="x(0) = -1.8")   # trajectory starting on the Pattern A side
ax.plot(t, x_B, color="tab:orange", label="x(0) = +1.8") # trajectory starting on the Pattern B side
ax.scatter([t0, t0], [x_A[0], x_B[0]], color=["tab:blue", "tab:orange"],
           zorder=3, clip_on=False)            # dots on the starting values x(0) = -1.8 and +1.8
for e in eq[stable]:                           # one dashed line per stable equilibrium
    ax.axhline(e, color="black", lw=0.8, ls="--")          # horizontal reference line at the stable equilibrium
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8)            # horizontal line x = 0 (unstable equilibrium, no preference)

ticks = [x_A[0], eq[0], eq[1], eq[2], x_B[0]]  # starting values and the 3 equilibria, all taken from the computed results
ax.set_yticks(ticks)                           # places the ticks exactly at these values
ax.set_yticklabels([str(round(float(v), 3)) for v in ticks])  # labels computed from the values, rounded to 3 decimals

ax.set_xlabel("Time t (dimensionless)")        # horizontal axis label (time has no unit in this model)
ax.set_ylabel("Coordination preference x")     # vertical axis label (same wording as Section 3)
ax.set_xlim(t0, t_end)                         # shows the whole simulation, from t = 0 to t = 20
ax.legend(loc="center right")                  # legend placed where it does not hide the curves
plt.show()                                     # displays the figure
```

@fig-baseline-trajectories shows how the coordination preference changes over time for two different starting values. The horizontal axis shows the time $t$ and the vertical axis shows the coordination preference $x$. The blue line shows the simulation starting from $x(0) = -1.8$, while the orange line shows the simulation starting from $x(0) = +1.8$. The dashed black lines show the two stable equilibria, while the grey line shows the unstable equilibrium.

 We can see that the two trajectories behave in opposite but symmetrical ways. For both, the preference evolves quickly at first, but then slows down as it approaches a stable equilibrium. When starting at $x(0) = -1.8$, the preference increases and then becomes constant. When starting at $x(0) = +1.8$, the preference decreases and becomes constant. Both trajectories become constant after $t \approx 1.5$.

The two simulations reach different final preferences: approximately $-1.225$ for the negative starting value and approximately $+1.225$ for the positive starting value. These final values are consistent with the two stable equilibria identified in Section 3 (@fig-baseline-vector). Furthermore, neither of the trajectories crosses $x=0$. The simulations are therefore consistent with the stability analysis.

In terms of movement coordination, the two stable equilibria act as attractors. Indeed, the athlete starting at $x(0) = -1.8$ settles into a stable preference for Pattern A, while the athlete starting at $x(0) = +1.8$ settles into a stable preference for Pattern B. While their preferences become less extreme over time, they do not switch to the other pattern. Consequently, without any instruction, the starting preference determines which stable state is reached.

## Numerical implementation check

In this part, we will check the numerical implementation. First, we verify that the number of Euler steps is correct. The simulation runs from $t = 0$ to $t = 20$, with a step size of $h = 0.01$. This means that there should be $20 / 0.01 = 2000$ steps. Including the starting point, there should be 2001 time values. This was confirmed in Python with `len(t)`, which returns 2001.

We then check the final values of both simulations. The simulation starting from $x(0) = -1.8$ ends at $x(20) \approx -1.2247$, and the simulation starting from $x(0) = +1.8$ ends at $x(20) \approx +1.2247$. These values match the stable equilibria found in Section 3. 

These checks are useful to confirm that the simulation uses the correct settings and that the numerical results agree with the graphical analysis from Section 3.

In the next section, we will repeat this analysis but with an external instruction of $I = 0.70$. We will compare how the stable preferences and simulation results change with this new condition.

```{python}

print("Final value from x(0) = -1.8:", round(x_A[-1], 4))   # should be close to -1.225
print("Final value from x(0) = +1.8:", round(x_B[-1], 4))   # should be close to +1.225
print("Stable equilibria (Section 3):", np.round(eq[stable], 4))  # values to compare with
```
